assessment.name: Year 10 Design and Technology Autumn assessment (AQA GCSE)
assessment.sections: Wednesday 2 December, period 4. Written paper on core technical principles: multiple choice, short answers, calculations and longer explain questions.
assessment.weighting: Core technical principles: new technologies, energy, new and smart materials, systems, mechanical devices, and materials and their properties.

mock.note: 30 questions across all core technical principles. Then try the gear and lever calculations in the Written practice tab.

cards.title: Production techniques and systems
cards.question: How have new technologies changed how products are made?
points: Automation: machines and robots do repetitive tasks quickly, accurately and without breaks.
CAD (computer aided design) and CAM (computer aided manufacture) such as laser cutters, CNC routers and 3D printers.
Flexible manufacturing systems (FMS): machines that can be quickly changed to make different products.
Just in time (JIT): materials arrive only when needed, reducing storage costs. Lean manufacturing aims to cut all waste.
cards.watch_out: JIT reduces storage costs but depends on reliable suppliers. If a delivery is late, production stops.
cards.hook: JIT: just enough, just in time.
cards.grade9: Discuss the impact on people: automation improves quality but can reduce jobs and require new skills.

cards.title: Enterprise and new ways of selling
cards.question: What new business ideas help designers bring products to market?
points: Crowdfunding: many people each give a small amount of money online to fund a new product.
Virtual marketing and retail: selling online, social media advertising, influencers.
Co-operatives: businesses owned and run by their members, who share the profits.
Fair trade: producers in developing countries receive a fair price and decent working conditions.
cards.watch_out: Fair trade is about fair pay and conditions for producers, not about products being cheap.
cards.grade9: Evaluate crowdfunding: it tests demand before manufacture, but ideas can be copied once public.

cards.title: Sustainability and responsible design
cards.question: How do designers consider sustainability, the environment and society?
points: Finite resources will run out (oil, metals). Non finite resources can be replaced (timber from managed forests).
The 6 Rs: reduce, reuse, recycle, rethink, refuse, repair.
Planned obsolescence: designing products to fail or go out of date, so people buy new ones.
Design for maintenance: products that can be repaired, with standard parts and screws instead of glue.
cards.watch_out: Recycling still uses energy. Reduce and reuse are usually better for the environment.
cards.hook: Rethink, Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repair, Recycle: best first.
cards.grade9: Use life cycle assessment (materials, manufacture, use, disposal) to judge a product's full environmental impact.

cards.title: Fossil fuels and nuclear power
cards.question: How is electricity generated from fossil fuels and nuclear fuel, and what are the issues?
points: Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) are burned to heat water into steam, which turns turbines connected to generators.
They are reliable and can meet demand quickly, but release carbon dioxide and are finite.
Nuclear power uses the heat from splitting uranium atoms (fission) to make steam.
Nuclear produces no carbon dioxide while running, but creates radioactive waste and is expensive to build and decommission.
cards.watch_out: Nuclear fuel is finite too. It is low carbon, not renewable.
cards.grade9: Weigh reliability against environmental cost when comparing energy sources.

cards.title: Renewable energy and energy storage
cards.question: What are the main renewable energy sources, and how is energy stored?
points: Renewables: wind, solar (photovoltaic), tidal, hydroelectric, biomass. They will not run out.
Drawbacks: some are unreliable (wind, solar) and need large areas or affect wildlife.
Kinetic pumped storage: water is pumped uphill when demand is low, then released through turbines at peak times (for example Dinorwig in Wales).
Batteries: alkaline batteries are single use; rechargeable batteries (lithium ion, NiMH) can be reused many times.
cards.watch_out: Biomass releases carbon dioxide when burned, but is called carbon neutral because the plants absorbed it while growing.
cards.grade9: Explain why storage matters for renewables: it stores energy when the wind blows and releases it when it does not.

cards.title: Choosing a power source for a product
cards.question: How do designers choose between batteries, mains and renewable power for a product?
points: Batteries make products portable but need replacing or recharging and create waste.
Mains power is constant but limits where the product can be used.
Small solar cells or wind up generators can power low energy products such as calculators, torches and radios.
Consider cost, convenience, energy needs and environmental impact.
cards.watch_out: Rechargeable batteries cost more at first but are cheaper and greener over the product's life.
cards.grade9: Justify a choice for a named product, such as a solar garden light, with at least two reasons.

cards.title: Modern materials
cards.question: What are graphene, metal foams, titanium and nanomaterials, and what are they used for?
points: Graphene: a sheet of carbon one atom thick. Extremely strong, light and conductive. Uses: electronics, batteries.
Metal foams: metal with gas bubbles inside. Light, absorb impact energy. Uses: car crash structures.
Titanium: strong, lightweight, corrosion resistant and biocompatible. Uses: hip replacements, aircraft parts.
Nanomaterials: tiny particles that give new properties, such as self cleaning glass or antibacterial coatings.
Liquid crystal displays (LCDs) use liquid crystals that change when a voltage is applied.
cards.watch_out: Modern materials are developed through new processes; they do not react to their environment like smart materials do.
cards.grade9: Link each property to a reason for its use, such as biocompatible, so the body does not reject a titanium implant.

cards.title: Smart materials
cards.question: What are smart materials, and which three should you know?
points: Smart materials change a property in response to a change in their environment (heat, light, stress), and the change is reversible.
Shape memory alloys (such as nitinol) return to their original shape when heated. Uses: glasses frames, dental braces.
Thermochromic pigments change colour with temperature. Uses: baby feeding spoons, kettle indicators, mugs.
Photochromic pigments change colour with light (UV). Uses: lenses that darken in sunlight.
cards.watch_out: Thermo means heat; photo means light. Mixing them up is the most common error.
cards.hook: Thermo = thermometer = heat. Photo = photograph = light.
cards.grade9: Explain why a thermochromic spoon improves safety: it shows when food is too hot for a baby.

cards.title: Composite materials
cards.question: What are composite materials and why are they used?
points: A composite combines two or more materials to get better properties than either alone.
Glass reinforced plastic (GRP): glass fibres in polyester resin. Strong, light, waterproof. Uses: boat hulls, car bodies.
Carbon fibre reinforced plastic (CFRP): carbon fibres in epoxy resin. Very strong, very light, expensive. Uses: racing bikes, Formula 1 cars.
Other composites: plywood and MDF (timber), concrete with steel reinforcement.
cards.watch_out: The fibres give strength; the resin (matrix) holds the fibres together and gives shape.
cards.grade9: Compare GRP and CFRP: CFRP is stronger and lighter but costs much more, so it is used where weight matters most.

cards.title: Technical textiles
cards.question: What are technical textiles and how are they used?
points: Technical textiles are designed for performance, not only for appearance.
Kevlar (an aramid fibre): very strong and heat resistant. Uses: body armour, cut resistant gloves.
Conductive fabrics carry electricity. Uses: touchscreen gloves, heated clothing.
Fire resistant fabrics (such as Nomex) for firefighters; breathable waterproof membranes (such as Gore-Tex); microfibres for sportswear.
Microencapsulation: tiny capsules in fabric release fragrance, moisturiser or antibacterial agents.
cards.watch_out: Kevlar is strong because of its fibre structure, but it is still a textile, not a metal.
cards.grade9: Match fabrics to user needs: a mountain jacket needs breathability, waterproofing and low weight.

cards.title: Systems: input, process, output
cards.question: What is a systems approach to designing electronic products?
points: Input: sensors and switches detect a change. Process: a control device decides what to do. Output: something happens.
Input devices: light dependent resistor (LDR, light), thermistor (temperature), pressure pads, push and toggle switches.
Process devices: microcontrollers (programmable chips, such as a PIC) that can be reprogrammed.
Output devices: lamps and LEDs (light), buzzers and speakers (sound), motors (movement).

example.heading: Night light system
lines: Process: microcontroller checks the light level

cards.watch_out: An LDR's resistance goes down as light increases. A thermistor's resistance usually goes down as temperature rises.
cards.grade9: Explain why microcontrollers are useful: one chip replaces many parts, and it can be reprogrammed to change how the product works.

cards.title: Types of motion
cards.question: What are the four types of motion?
points: Linear: moving in a straight line in one direction (a paper trimmer blade, a train on a straight track).
Reciprocating: moving backwards and forwards in a straight line (a sewing machine needle, a jigsaw blade).
Rotary: moving in a circle (a wheel, a drill).
Oscillating: swinging back and forth in an arc (a pendulum, a swing).
cards.watch_out: Reciprocating is back and forth in a straight line; oscillating is back and forth in a curve.
cards.hook: Lines, Returns, Rotates, Oscillates: straight, back and forth, round, swing.
cards.grade9: Name the mechanism that changes one motion into another, such as a cam changing rotary into reciprocating.

cards.title: Levers and mechanical advantage
cards.question: What are the three classes of lever, and how do you calculate mechanical advantage?
points: First class: fulcrum in the middle (see saw, crowbar, scissors).
Second class: load in the middle (wheelbarrow, nutcracker, bottle opener).
Third class: effort in the middle (tweezers, fishing rod, human forearm).
Mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort. A value above 1 means the lever makes the job easier.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: A load of 600 N is lifted with an effort of 200 N

cards.watch_out: Mechanical advantage has no units because it is a ratio of two forces.
cards.hook: FLE 123: Fulcrum, Load, Effort in the middle for classes 1, 2, 3.
cards.grade9: Third class levers have an MA below 1, but they give greater movement and speed at the load.

cards.title: Linkages
cards.question: What do linkages do, and which ones should you know?
points: Linkages transfer force and change the direction of motion.
Reverse motion linkage: the output moves in the opposite direction to the input.
Parallel motion linkage: the output moves in the same direction as the input (toolbox trays).
Bell crank: changes motion through 90 degrees (bicycle brakes).
Crank and slider: changes rotary motion into reciprocating motion (engine pistons).
cards.watch_out: The fixed pivot does not move; moving pivots move with the linkage. Draw them differently.
cards.grade9: Moving the fixed pivot changes how far the output moves. Closer to the output means less movement but more force.

cards.title: Cams and followers
cards.question: How do cams and followers work?
points: A cam rotates and the follower rests on it, changing rotary motion into reciprocating motion.
Pear cam: the follower is still (dwells) for half a turn, then rises and falls.
Eccentric (offset circle) cam: smooth, continuous rise and fall.
Snail (drop) cam: slow rise, then a sudden drop. It can only turn one way.
Followers: knife (accurate but wears), flat (hard wearing), roller (low friction).
cards.watch_out: A snail cam must rotate in one direction only, or the follower jams on the drop.
cards.grade9: Choose a cam for a purpose: a snail cam for a sudden pop up movement in a toy.

cards.title: Gears and pulleys
cards.question: How do gear trains and pulleys change speed and force, and how do you calculate ratios?
points: Gear ratio = teeth on driven gear ÷ teeth on driver gear.
Output speed = input speed ÷ gear ratio.
Two meshing spur gears turn in opposite directions. An idler gear makes them turn the same way.
Pulley velocity ratio = diameter of driven pulley ÷ diameter of driver pulley. Pulleys on a belt turn the same way.
Other gears: bevel gears turn motion through 90 degrees; rack and pinion turns rotary into linear; worm and wheel gives a big reduction.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: Driver 20 teeth, driven 60 teeth: ratio = 60 ÷ 20 = 3, written 3 : 1

cards.watch_out: Driven over driver. Putting the driver on top gives the wrong ratio.
cards.hook: Driven over driver: big driven gear, slow but strong.
cards.grade9: For compound gears, multiply the ratios of each pair to find the overall ratio.

cards.title: Papers and boards
cards.question: What are the main papers and boards, and their uses?
points: Paper is measured in gsm (grams per square metre). Over about 170 gsm it is usually called board.
Copier paper (80 gsm) for printing; cartridge paper for drawing; tracing paper; layout paper for design ideas.
Corrugated card: strong, light, insulating; used for packaging boxes.
Duplex board for food packaging; foil lined board for takeaway lids; foam board for models; solid white board for high quality packaging.
cards.watch_out: Corrugated card is strong for its weight because the fluted middle layer acts like a beam.
cards.grade9: Choose packaging by properties: a pizza box needs grease resistance, insulation and strength, so corrugated card.

cards.title: Timbers
cards.question: What are hardwoods, softwoods and manufactured boards?
points: Hardwoods come from deciduous trees (broad leaves, lose them in autumn). Slow growing, often expensive. Oak, beech, mahogany, ash, balsa.
Softwoods come from coniferous trees (needles, evergreen). Faster growing, cheaper. Pine, spruce, larch, cedar.
Manufactured boards: MDF (smooth, no grain, easy to paint), plywood (layers at right angles, strong), chipboard (cheap, used in flat pack).
Manufactured boards come in large, stable sheets and use waste wood.
cards.watch_out: Balsa is a hardwood, even though it is very soft. The name comes from the tree type, not hardness.
cards.hook: Hard = deciduous (drops leaves). Soft = coniferous (cones and needles).
cards.grade9: Explain why plywood is strong: each layer's grain is at 90 degrees to the next, so it resists splitting.

cards.title: Metals and alloys
cards.question: What are ferrous metals, non ferrous metals and alloys?
points: Ferrous metals contain iron, are usually magnetic and can rust: mild steel, cast iron, high carbon steel.
Non ferrous metals contain no iron and do not rust: aluminium (light, used for cans), copper (conducts electricity), tin, zinc.
Alloys are mixtures of metals (or a metal and another element) for better properties.
Brass = copper + zinc. Bronze = copper + tin. Stainless steel = steel + chromium (and nickel), which resists corrosion.
cards.watch_out: Stainless steel contains iron, so it is a ferrous alloy, but chromium stops it rusting.
cards.hook: Ferrous comes from Fe, the chemical symbol for iron.
cards.grade9: Link properties to products: aluminium for drinks cans because it is light, malleable, recyclable and does not corrode.

cards.title: Polymers
cards.question: What is the difference between thermoforming and thermosetting polymers?
points: Thermoforming polymers soften when heated and can be reshaped many times. Acrylic, HIPS, PET, PVC, polypropylene.
Thermosetting polymers set permanently when first heated; they cannot be reshaped. Epoxy resin, melamine formaldehyde, polyester resin, urea formaldehyde.
Thermoforming polymers can be recycled more easily.
Thermosetting polymers resist heat, so they are used for pan handles, plug sockets and kitchen worktops.
cards.watch_out: Acrylic is thermoforming, which is why it can be line bent on a strip heater.
cards.hook: Thermosetting sets once; thermoforming forms again and again.
cards.grade9: Explain using structure: thermosetting polymers have cross links between chains, so heat cannot soften them.

cards.title: Textiles
cards.question: What are natural, synthetic and blended fibres, and how are fabrics made?
points: Natural fibres: cotton (plant, absorbent, breathable), wool (animal, warm, crease resistant), silk (animal, smooth, lustrous).
Synthetic fibres from oil: polyester (strong, crease resistant), polyamide or nylon (hard wearing), elastane (very stretchy).
Blends combine fibres for better properties, such as polycotton: cotton comfort plus polyester's crease resistance.
Fabric construction: woven (interlaced threads, strong), knitted (looped yarn, stretchy), non woven (bonded fibres such as felt).
cards.watch_out: Fibres are the tiny hairs; yarns are spun from fibres; fabrics are made from yarns.
cards.grade9: Justify a fabric choice for a product, such as a PE kit, using two properties.

cards.title: Working and physical properties
cards.question: What do the key material properties mean?
points: Strength: withstands a force without breaking. Hardness: resists scratching and wear.
Toughness: absorbs impact without breaking. Its opposite is brittleness.
Malleability: can be hammered or pressed into shape. Ductility: can be stretched into wire.
Elasticity: returns to its original shape after a force is removed.
Physical properties also include density, absorbency, and thermal and electrical conductivity.
cards.watch_out: Hard and tough are not the same. Glass is hard but brittle, so it is not tough.
cards.grade9: Use precise property words in answers about material choice; examiners reward accurate terms over vague words like strong.

cards.title: Calculations and key lists
cards.question: Can you recall the formulas and lists you need?
points: Mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort.
Gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth. Output speed = input speed ÷ ratio.
Lever classes: fulcrum, load, effort in the middle for 1, 2, 3.
Smart materials: shape memory alloy, thermochromic, photochromic.
Thermoforming can be reheated; thermosetting cannot.
cards.watch_out: Show the formula, the substitution and the answer with units for full marks.

written.q: A driver gear with 15 teeth turns a driven gear with 45 teeth. The driver turns at 240 rpm. (a) Calculate the gear ratio. (b) Calculate the output speed.
model: Gear ratio = driven ÷ driver = 45 ÷ 15 (1)
= 3, written 3 : 1 (1)
Output speed = 240 ÷ 3 (1)

written.q: A bottle opener lifts a load of 90 N with an effort of 30 N. Name the class of lever and calculate the mechanical advantage.
model: Second class lever (1)
MA = load ÷ effort = 90 ÷ 30 (1)

written.q: Explain how smart materials could be used in products for babies and young children.
model: Smart materials respond reversibly to a change in their surroundings (1)
Thermochromic pigment in a feeding spoon changes colour if food is too hot (1)
This protects the baby from burns (1)
Thermochromic strips in bath toys show if water is too hot (1)
Shape memory alloy in glasses frames returns to shape if bent (1)
Useful because young children often bend or sit on glasses (1)

written.q: Explain the difference between thermoforming and thermosetting polymers, giving one example of each.
model: Thermoforming polymers can be reheated and reshaped many times (1)
Example: acrylic, HIPS or PET (1)
Thermosetting polymers set permanently and cannot be reshaped (1)
Example: melamine formaldehyde, epoxy resin or urea formaldehyde (1)

written.q: Evaluate the use of renewable energy sources to generate electricity in the UK.
model: Renewables will not run out, unlike fossil fuels (1)
They produce little or no carbon dioxide when generating (1)
Wind and solar are unreliable, depending on weather (1)
Energy storage such as pumped storage or batteries is needed (1)
Some have environmental impacts, such as tidal barrages on habitats (1)
Justified conclusion weighing the points (1)

exam_tips.timing: About a minute per mark. Do calculations carefully and check them.

section_a.Multiple choice: cover the options and answer first.

section_a: Learn the examples for each material and each lever class.
section_b: Explain questions need a reason linked to a property or a user need.
Use precise words such as malleable, ductile and biocompatible.
grade9: Link properties to products and users in every material answer.
In evaluate questions give advantages, disadvantages and a judgement.
Draw labelled sketches if they help to explain mechanisms.

vocab.meaning: Able to be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking
vocab.example: Aluminium is malleable, so it is easy to press into cans.

vocab.meaning: Able to be drawn out into a thin wire
vocab.example: Copper is ductile, which makes it ideal for electrical wire.
Titanium is biocompatible, so it is used in hip replacements.

vocab.meaning: Able to continue without harming the environment for the future
vocab.example: Using timber from managed forests is more sustainable.

vocab.meaning: The state of being out of date or no longer useful
vocab.example: Planned obsolescence encourages people to buy new phones.

vocab.meaning: A material made from two or more materials combined
vocab.example: Carbon fibre reinforced plastic is a composite.

vocab.meaning: Using machines and robots to do work automatically
vocab.example: Automation makes production faster and more consistent.
A thermochromic spoon warns when food is too hot.

vocab.meaning: Moving backwards and forwards in a straight line
vocab.example: A jigsaw blade has a reciprocating motion.

vocab.meaning: The pivot point of a lever
vocab.example: In a see saw the fulcrum is in the middle.
